Let’s dive into Chapter 9: Overcoming Organizational Barriers.
Even when you’ve got a clear handle on what your customers really want, there’s one hurdle that can trip up even the best teams—internal resistance. I mean, legacy processes, old reward systems, and a natural fear of risk can all get in the way when you’re trying to move from a product-focused mindset to actually thinking about the jobs your customers need done.
So, how do you break through those barriers?
First off, leadership needs to lead the charge. When leaders make the jobs approach a top priority—and actually reward teams for putting customers at the center of innovation—it sends a powerful message. It tells everyone, “Hey, this is important.”
Next, it’s all about creating safe spaces for experimentation. Imagine a place where trying something new isn’t risky—it’s expected. Here, failure isn’t a scarlet letter; it’s a chance to learn and improve. That shift in mindset changes everything.
And don’t forget about incentives. If you want people to focus on customer jobs, you’ve got to align rewards and recognition with progress in that area—not just with quick financial wins.
Here’s a real-world example to bring this to life: A consumer electronics company realized their bonus system was all about launching new features, but not about whether those features actually helped customers. So, they switched things up. Instead of just counting launches, they started tracking how many customers could set up their product in less than ten minutes. Suddenly, teams were laser-focused on making things easier for real people. That’s the power of changing what you measure and reward.
Of course, change is never simple. But you know what? Small wins add up. Every time you celebrate a story of a customer making progress—even if it’s just a tiny step—you build momentum. Those moments reinforce why the jobs approach matters, and they inspire others across the organization to get onboard.
So, the big takeaway? Overcoming organizational barriers isn’t about one big leap. It’s about steady steps, strong leadership, and a culture that’s genuinely excited about helping customers succeed.
